title: True God and true man (CCC 464–469)
hook: fully God and fully human, not a mixture

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Incarnation: the Word made flesh. Your line was god with skin. Did you get hungry, or tired, and remember? Today, the question it raises: how can one person be both? Day three hundred four.

One person, both God and human. The mind reaches for a shortcut. Maybe he was God wearing a human costume, like a king in disguise. Maybe he was a very holy man God adopted. Maybe he was half and half, like a centaur, or a blend, like coffee with milk, where you can't find either one anymore. Versions of those shortcuts were tried in the early Church, and argued over in councils and letters. And the Church said no to them. What it said instead fits in five words.
screen: `A KING IN DISGUISE?` → `HALF AND HALF?` → `COFFEE WITH MILK?`

segments.voice: The council's word: Chalcedon. First, not part and part. The Catechism is plain: Jesus is not partly God and partly human, and not a confused mixture of the two. He is fully both. Second, the councils. In the year 451, bishops met at Chalcedon and wrote the careful version: one person, the Son of God, in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Four withouts, each one closing a door on a shortcut. Some ancient churches, like the Coptic and Armenian churches, have put the faith in different words, and in recent decades their leaders and the popes have signed statements saying they share the same faith in Christ. Third, what fully human means. It means a human body, and also a human mind that learned, and a human will, and human feelings. The Gospels don't hide them. In Mark, he looks around at people "with anger, being grieved for the blindness of their hearts." A rich man runs up and kneels before him, and Mark says Jesus looked at him and loved him. In the garden, he says: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." And at his friend Lazarus's tomb, in John, three plain words:"And Jesus wept." Fourth, why it matters on a Tuesday. The letter to the Hebrews says Christians don't have a high priest who can't feel what they feel, but "one tempted in all things like as we are, without sin." The loneliness, the grief, the anger at unfairness, the dread before something hard. Catholics say none of it is foreign to him.
screen: `NOT PART AND PART. NOT A BLEND.` · `CHALCEDON, 451: FOUR WITHOUTS.` · `ANGER, LOVE, SORROW, TEARS.` · `TEMPTED IN ALL THINGS, WITHOUT SIN.` · then, large: `AND JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice his human emotions. Settle, and breathe. Pick one of the four moments: the anger at hard hearts, the love for the rich man, the sorrow in the garden, the tears at the tomb. Picture it. His face. Then find the same feeling somewhere in your own week. When were you angry at something unfair? When did grief catch you? Set your moment next to his. If you pray, you can talk to him about it, as someone who knows. The bell holds the time.
Chalcedon, the council in 451 that defined Jesus as one person, truly God and truly human, without confusion or division. Today's word.
Your line: he felt what you feel. Today, when a strong feeling hits, name it, and remember one Gospel moment when he felt it too. Day three hundred four.

howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed that Christ is true God and true man, and some meditate on his human feelings in the Gospels, especially in Lent and in the Sorrowful Mysteries of the rosary.

fork.setup: you're at the council of Chalcedon in 451. someone proposes that Christ's divinity and humanity blend into one new thing. what does the council say?
options: no: one person, two natures, without confusion.

fork.reveal: the council said one person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation: closing the door on both a blend and a split.

original.note: Latin: truly God, truly man, the Western Church's summary of Chalcedon.

trapdoor: what you thought: God in a human costume.
what it means: one person, fully divine and fully human, with a real human mind, will and feelings.
what a scholar hears: Chalcedon's four adverbs, without confusion, change, division, separation; the non-Chalcedonian churches and the modern joint declarations.

Joint christological statements: Paul VI and Coptic Pope Shenouda III (1973), John Paul II and Armenian Catholicos Karekin I (1996). Keeper should confirm the one-line summary is fair to the Oriental Orthodox churches.
'Shortest verse in the Bible' is true of English Bibles (John 11:35); in other languages other verses can be shorter.
